In the US, there are certain kinds of laws congresses can't pass, actions that executives can't take, and decisions that ordinary citizens can't make -today I'm talking about what're generally described as protected classes plus whatever the US Constitution says you can't do to citizens.

There is a problem with this, though: What do you do if there is a strong demographic correlation between a protected class and some non-protected feature?

  1. If you do nothing, nefarious policymakers can make laws that discriminate against the un-protected class and still effectively achieve legal discrimination against a protected class!
  2. If you accept correlated discrimination as discrimination against a protected class, nefarious citizens can comb though demographics to find some correlation among the affected population of a policy they just don't like, and claim that the policy discriminates against a protected class to get it thrown out.

Example 1: Employee Benefits & Compensation during Pregnancy

For example, this excerpt from the text of the US' Civil Rights Act of 1964:

...

DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF RACE, COLOR, RELIGION, SEX, OR NATIONAL ORIGIN SEC. 703.

(a) It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer--

(1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin; or

...

Original Interpretation

In 1974ish, in the state of California:

California has a disability insurance system for private employees temporarily disabled from working by an injury or illness not covered by workmen's compensation, under which an employee contributes to an Unemployment Compensation Disability Fund one percent of his salary up to an annual maximum of $85. A disability lasting less than eight days is not compensable, except when the employee is hospitalized. Benefits are not payable for a single disability exceeding 26 weeks. A disability resulting from an individual's court commitment as a dipsomaniac, drug addict, or sexual psychopath is not compensable, nor are certain disabilities attributable to pregnancy.

Excluding coverage for stuff caused by pregnancy? Was this illegal sex-based discrimination against women?

That question was argued before the US Supreme Court in Geduldig v. Aiello 417 U.S. 484 (1974), and the USSC said no:

The program does not discriminate with respect to the persons or groups eligible for its protection, ...

In other words, "let me check the law... yeah, "pregnant people" aren't listed as a protected class, so, no, that's not illegal. In a second case in 1976, General Electric Co. v. Gilbert, 429 U. S. 125, the USSC reaffirmed this interpretation.

Revision

The US Congress didn't like this and later passed the Pregnancy Discrimination Act in 1978, explicitly codifying the protection of pregnant people, invalidating the USSC's ruling, which the USSC affirmed in Newport News Shipbuilding Co. v. EEOC, 462 U.S. 669 (1983).

In light of the new law, the USSC ruled

(a) Congress, by enacting the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, not only overturned the holding of General Electric Co. v. Gilbert, 429 U. S. 125, that the exclusion of disabilities caused by pregnancy from an employer's disability plan providing general coverage did not constitute discrimination based on sex, but also rejected the reasoning employed in that case that differential treatment of pregnancy is not gender-based discrimination because only women can become pregnant.

The Point

  1. The courts rejected the argument that discriminating based on pregnancy is illegal because only women can become pregnant, therefore it is discrimination based on sex.
  2. The people's duly-elected representatives realized this wasn't the outcome they'd intended, and passed new laws for the courts to interpret, thereby getting everyone on the same page as to what the laws did and didn't mean.

Example 2: Texas Voter ID Laws

This hasn't made it to the US Supreme Court yet.

In 2011, the Texas Legislature passed SB 14 which introduced stricter laws regarding the types of ID that were acceptable to permit someone to vote in the state of Texas.

Basically, you had to have one of the following to be allowed to vote:

  1. Valid, un-expired Texas Driver's License
  2. Valid, un-expired Texas ID Card
  3. US Military Photo ID card, no more than 60 days expired
  4. US Citizenship Certificate with photo
  5. US Passport, no more than 60 days expired
  6. Valid Texas Concealed Handgun License, no more than 60 days expired
  7. A Valid Texas-Issued Election Identification Certificate (basically a free ID that is only valid for getting you into elections). To get one of these, you had to not have any of the other forms of ID, and do one of the following
    1. Be federally registered to vote in Texas and present your federal voter registration certificate
    2. Fill out a form per Texas Election Code 13.001, which I couldn't be bothered to look up and link.

This law was almost immediately challenged as being racially discriminatory. What!? How do you get race out of that text?

So far, every court up to the US 5th Circuit Court of Appeals in Texas NAACP v. Steen has upheld the original finding in Texas v. Holder that

...

Ample circumstantial evidence exists that SB 14 was passed with discriminatory purpose.

...

TEXAS HAS FAILED TO PROVE THAT SENATE BILL 14 DOES NOT HAVE A RETROGRESSIVE EFFECT.

...

The Only Plausible and Credible Evidence Before the Court Establishes that SB 14 Will Have a Retrogressive Effect on Minority Voters

...

The Point

This ruling establishes 3 concepts:

  1. We aren't fooled by your pretext of protecting elections - we know you just hate minorities, Texas Legislature
  2. It is unconstitutional to pass a law which causes some people who can currently vote, from being able to vote in the future, no exceptions.
  3. There is a strong correlation between "people who will be unable to vote under this law" and "non-whites." Therefore, this law does in fact discriminate based on race.

Summary

What do you do if there is a strong demographic correlation between a protected class and some non-protected feature?

  1. If you do nothing, nefarious policymakers can make laws that discriminate against the un-protected class and still effectively achieve legal discrimination against a protected class!
  2. If you accept correlated discrimination as discrimination against a protected class, nefarious citizens can comb though demographics to find some correlation among the affected population of a policy they just don't like, and claim that the policy discriminates against a protected class to get it thrown out.

In my opinion, the pregnancy issue was handled correctly: the USSC found that sex was a protected characteristic, and legislating against "pregnant people" didn't violate the law as written, because "pregnant people" weren't listed as a protected class. When the popular opinion was that this was wrong, the people's duly-elected representatives passed new legislation, which the court then re-interpreted in agreement with Congress' intentions. Certainly, in the actual cases brought, nefarious individuals were actually trying to underhandedly discriminate against women - or at least get away with not having to accommodate them. It helped that there is literally a perfect correlation between between pregnant people and females.

In my opinion, the Texas Voter ID issue has been handled dangerously:

  1. Actually OK, even though I personally disagree with the finding. One of the courts' job is to keep an eye out for nefarious policymakers attempting to underhandedly discriminate.
  2. This implies that if ever a mistake were made and people who shouldn't be allowed to vote, voted, it's not permissible to correct the mistake with legislation, and these people who shouldn't vote must be allowed to continue to be able to vote. This makes it impossible for the people's duly-elected representatives to pass laws that clarify & change the interpretation: a significant power is stripped from the elected representatives (which is bad), and then multiple powers that are supposed to keep each other in balance are being consolidated into just the courts (which is bad).
  3. The courts are affirming that if there is any correlation between the affected population of a policy, and a protected class, then that policy does indeed discriminate against a protected class and must the thrown out. Unfortunately, correlations are everywhere and frequently meaningless.

TL;DR

I would like to see the USSC answer the following Yes/No question: If there is a strong demographic correlation between a protected class and some non-protected attribute, do laws that discriminate against the non-protected attribute de facto discriminate against the protected class?
I would like to see the US Supreme Court rule on laws where the demographics of a "protected class" strongly correlate with non-protected attributes.
